newsitem.title: ROMANIA: ROMANIAN LEU DIPS AGAINST DOLLAR, SEEKS LEVEL.
newsitem.headline: ROMANIAN LEU DIPS AGAINST DOLLAR, SEEKS LEVEL.

text.p: Romania's leu currency dipped around three percent against the dollar on Tuesday, a slide seen by traders as the first sign of the new reformist government's commitment to allow it to find more realistic levels.
The leu slipped to 3,880/3,930 to the dollar from 3,780/3,800 in early trading. But it was still well above rates of 4,750 at Bucharest street currency shops.
"This means they want to take the bull by the horns rather than fool around with reforms," said one trader.
"It's a sign that the stabilisation programme is under way," echoed another.
The leu has been held artificially high since March, when the former leftist government restricted the local currency market to four market-making dealer banks.

That move obliged all banks taking part in market operations to observe rates imposed by the four selected banks, three of which were state-run. But the four appeared to have been more flexible in allowing the leu to fall in recent days.
The downward move began to gather pace in the past week with a five percent drop as the new administration took office after ousting ex-communists in last month's election.

Virtually everyone in Romania sees the street price as the leu's true value. That price is all but recognised by the interbank market, where cross trading in other currencies, like the German mark or French franc, produces considerably weaker leu-dollar rates.
Traders said the interbank leu-dollar rate would slip further but was unlikely to weaken beyond 4,000 this year.
"I guess it will end the year quiet but by February we might see it at 4,300-4,500," said one trader.

Attempts to prop up the leu artificially in an election year and restrictions on the foreign exchange market were among the reasons behind the International Monetary Fund's suspension of a three-year credit of $460 million earlier this year.

The cabinet's stabilisation package includes liberalisation of the foreign exchange market, one of the urgent measures recommended by the IMF after a visit last week by a technical team to evaluate the economy.
Banking sources said the central bank was expected to tighten its monetary policy by raising the discount rate, now at an annual 35 percent, to make it positive in real terms.
Year-on-year inflation was 47.4 percent in November, well above the 20 percent agreed with the IMF for 1996.
The Fund has also urged Romania to rein in budget expenditure, eliminate financing the farming sector through the central bank and raise petrol and energy prices.
The Fund's Managing Director, Michel Camdessus, is due in Bucharest this week ahead of negotiations in January on a new standby arrangement. REUTER
